## Data Documentation

- It is important to have documentation of your project, especially when collaborating with others
- One of my favorite resources
  - [Data Management in Large-Scale Education Research](https://datamgmtinedresearch.com/)
    - Level of aggregation and cleaning before sharing
- If using advisor's data, this becomes even more important since there could be legal issues if mistakes are made, like data leakage

## Documentation

- Variables
  - Make sure data types are stated
  - Variable types
  - Operationalization of variables
  - Units of measurement
  - Missing data
    - Missing data rules 
    - How data will be imputed

## Documentation

- Descriptions of workflows
- Access permissions fr specific variables
  - Unit of analysis level 
- Staying within the scope of regulating organizations (HIPAA)

## Codebook

- I like to have a specific file that has more information about each of my variables
- Codebooks are especially important for longitudinal data/cohort design tables
  - Makes data manipulation consistent across different data collection points
  - Also makes it transparent when mistakes are made
    - Coding of variables inconsistently happens
- Putting it in a Jupyter notebook/Quarto document allows for more organization

## Codebook Example

- We'll focus on the CESD, a common measure for depressive symptoms
  - [You can follow along here](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/014662167700100306)
- What to include
  - Name of variable(s)
    - variable name in dataset
  - Data type
  - Variable type
    - Recommendations for transformations
    - Scoring to make more sense --> new variable name(s)
  - Scale/Range of variable
  - Some people include descriptives (M, SD, range, etc.)
  - Skip logic in questions
  - Logical ways to get composite scores
    - Positive affect & Depressive symptoms
  - Rules for missing data
  - Amount of missing data
  - References (bibtex can be used in documents)
    - Articles of interest

## Codebook

- Include relevant information
  - Visualize missing data
  - Visualize distribution(s)
  - Render table(s) for potential problematic values
  - Define cutoffs from previous literature
  - Recoding based on previous literature

## Reproducibility & Open Source

- Having your code in a public space shows reproducibility

- Public repos showcase
  - Your code changes through commit history
  - Decision making
  - If you try to hide something
    - Setting a seed/state for analyses and then changing it
- Sharing everything about your project
  - May not be feasible for some of your projects
- Opens the door for collaborations with outside researchers

## Open Science

- Making research equitable by making everything in the research process more accessible
- Openly sharing
  - Software and code
  - Data*
  - Published research articles
  - APIs
- Makes it more reproducible too
  - When others have your code and data, they can double check your work to make sure the findings are accurate
- **Data may not always be completely raw**
  - Still need to protect identities for participants/subjects

## Open Science

- Making science open is expensive
  - To make a peer-reviewed article open access, it often costs thousands of dollars
  - Publishers guilt trip authors into wanting open access
  - Often negotiations between universities and publishers on price
-  Publishers want $, authors want to expand on literature
